problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & 5 \\ b & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of  $\frac{a}{b}.$

examples.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
examples.problem:
Consider the following matrices:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/7126688b8500e60258d29ab4b1b323ac956ad41b530c5723bcc71d60b11e73a0.png)
Given that $D=P^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}.$
examples.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/f3460b47901f79529216c1440403e2115ff9047cb997070893b241cd938728de.png) we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_2=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1= -{2}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/95d1bcb284138711bcf5afddb3f09c702e664fbdc7b256b0eaf81044f87403cf.png)

By setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/898d72a1a0cc123d1ff7ecb4c8d02f6951739a9498e36ff14ee44cb322952fb6.png)

Finally, $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{-2}{1} = -2.$

feedback.problem:
Determine if the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-4I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.
